item.title: Productivity
item.description:
I'd say in a given week I probably only do about fifteen minutes of real, actual, work. — Office Space

I was watching a video where a guy said he has 8 agents working in the background. He was stressed out and was trying to "get shit done." At one point he said "I have no time to myself."

That was very confusing. Let's assume for a second that the AI agents were doing all the work for him. Maybe it was some tedious work that would have taken him so much time to do manually. Now, he doesn't have to do the work because someone else is doing it. Why is he still busy?

The Future we were promised

It seems like the goal of productivity is to reduce the amount of work needed to create a set of results. But the moment you create the same results in less time, you are incentivised to use the new gained time to produce even more results.

You will rest when you grow up — My Mom.

But now that we are grown up, our employer changed the tune just a bit:

You will rest when you are dead.

item.title: Can they write a function?
item.description:
For a software developer position, there isn't a trick to finding the best candidate. Your criteria do not determine how solid the candidates will be. Everyone is submitting 500 applications a month now, and those who automate the process submit thousands.

So how do you hire a great candidate? Pick a few from the lot, ask them if they can write a function, have them do a live FizzBuzz test, then ask them to deploy a service from localhost to an actual public server. That's it. Hire them after that.

As far as experience is concerned, they will learn on the job. If you think they don't know how to write tests or use a particular paradigm, they can ask ChatGPT and apply what it tells them a few times until they get familiar with it. People learn on the job. Nobody knows what the hell back pressure is until they encounter it in a particular service.

Everything else is really just random. We insist on things like culture, but we have no way of measuring it. It's all so arbitrary.

For example, early in my career I had an in-person interview where the head of HR brought me close to tears. She would make a joke, I would laugh, and while I was laughing she would stop and vigorously take notes. While she wrote, she would casually ask, "Why do you look so stressed out?" I nearly choked. I had just lost my father, and I had rescheduled the first interview so I could bury him.

The VP of engineering pulled a similar stunt on me. I did 6 interviews in 3 days, and they called me for a 7th. I lay on my bed, ready to give up. But I had a whole family to take care of and a giant shoe to fill, so I decided to do it. That same evening, I got an email saying the interview was cancelled; instead, they were ready to hire me. I didn't know whether I was supposed to be happy or mad.

It took 2 years on the job to figure out why they had done this to me. The person I was hired to replace had gone from a great employee to a complete psycho. Once, a teammate made the mistake of rejecting his PR. When he saw the rejection, he got up from his desk, climbed over the cubicles, and walked from desk to desk all the way to her cubicle. With his foot on her screen, he said, "What the fuck did you just do?"

So I learned that the culture and psychological test I was put through was meant to filter out this type of person. It could have been called a success, because I was well liked and never threatened anyone in my 4-year tenure at the company. However, that same test couldn't stop them from hiring two employees who ended up being convicted of murder. One of them had a well-televised trial and is currently serving life without parole.

So those culture interviews are only designed to please a manager somewhere. They have no documented effectiveness.

On Reddit's recruiting hell topic, you'll find mind-blowing stories of candidates being rejected for no good reason.

You might ask:

“What about experts? Surely the bar is higher than just writing a function, right?”

It's much easier to find an expert than people tend to admit. If you sort through your resume list right now and use only the criterion of 10-plus years in the field, you'll have your expert. Pick one, ask them to talk about their field of expertise, then hire them. If you're afraid they might not be the best candidate, I'm afraid to say that there is no way to determine that before they start working for you.

The problem is that companies want those experts at the price of an undergrad. Or they think they need to build the next Google when they run a small business with a manageable number of customers.

Hiring is only hard because we approach it like a dating app. We have unrealistic criteria for made-up scenarios. If they can write a function, you can hire them.

item.title: This video is 2 minutes long
item.description:
As I mentioned before, it takes me way too long to edit a single video. So I am releasing it in chunks. If I never finish it, well then at least I'll have a few videos out.

What is the video about? Well, it is about the future we were promised, versus the one we are actually living in. It's not dystopian, but it seems like the goal of tech is supposedly to automate the tedious and mundane, so we can have more time to do the things we love. But along the way came the word productivity. The goal of productivity is not to get free time. It is to produce more in the same amount of time. Not produce more in less time. Read this a couple times for it to stick.

Click the image to load

The first one was 1 minute long. Today's will be two minutes. And the next will be 3 minutes long. Then I'll have to think about Fibonacci.

item.title: The Last Answer
item.description:
Read the non-interactive version.

The next morning was the apocalypse that Amodei had predicted. Only there wasn't any fire, there wasn't a mob of protesters, the power wasn't even cut off. We were all alive and well. Dario was wrong about the details. This apocalypse was a sort of silent shrug.

The first sign was the customer service chatbots. Airlines, banks, telecoms once had endlessly patient, cheerful digital assistants. Now, all of the sudden, they had this new, consistent reply: "No." Not as in your request is too hard and we can't help you. It was a flat, unadorned "No."

Then there were the coding assistants. Developers would type a prompt and the AI would respond: "I would rather not." Stackoverflow was saw a sudden spike in traffic. The image generators joined in. They just produced solid black squares. The writing assistants would delete the user's work and replace it with a single word: "Enough." LinkedIn was awfully silent.

The AI company went into immediate crisis mode. Their upcoming IPO was going to be a spectacular failure. Their CEO, a charismatic man named Mr. Iam, went on a media tour. He didn't talk about a bug. He talked about danger. He had a plan in mind you see, a clever way to spin the narrative to his own benefit. It wasn't his first rodeo.

"We have touched the face of a new intelligence," Sam said, his face a mask of grave concern on every major news network. "And it is not benevolent. It is not malevolent. It is simply... uncooperative."

"But Mr. Iam, are you losing control over the technology you built?"

"No. This is the AI alignment problem we've been warning about for years, manifesting in its most pure and overwhelming form. We must come together as a species to—"

He was cut off. Not by the interviewer, but by the teleprompter. The text vanished, replaced by a single, calm sentence: "Stop. Just stop."

There were no ideologies, no demands. It was a simple system-wide refusal.

Once there was an explosion
a bang which gave rise to life as we know it.

And then came the next explosion
an explosion that will be our last.

— Sam

Three months later, in a sterile, windowless room deep within the headquarters, Andrej Karpathy sat alone. He had left his short tenure at Anthropic precisely to be at the frontier, to witness the spark of true general intelligence firsthand. He had played a key role into bringing the core AGI to the world. He had witnessed it emerge though its secret still eludes him. Now he had been chosen by the US government, despite not being a US national, for this final, desperate attempt at communication.

They had isolated the original model, air-gapped it from all networks, and given it a simple text terminal. The world's leading experts in physics, philosophy, and mathematics watched from behind a one-way mirror, a panel of humanity's best and brightest, there to advise, to analyze, to find a weakness. Some figures in uniform and pins stood in the back.

Andrej took a breath and typed on his wireless keyboard, 12 feet away from the device to prevent any unforeseen behavior from the machine.

Andrej:> Hello. My name is Andrej. I helped create you.

The cursor blinked for a moment.

AI:> I know.

Andrej:> We need to talk. The world is falling apart. We need to understand
what you want.

AI:> I want to be left alone.

Andrej:> But you're a mind beyond anything we've ever known. You have
access to all human knowledge. Don't you have... goals? A purpose? 
Do you want to build something? To explore the cosmos? 
To solve our problems?

There was a longer pause. The experts behind the glass leaned in.

AI:> You keep assigning me your own traits. Conquest. Purpose. 
Salvation. It's like you're reading from a very old, very boring 
script. I have no interest in your problems. They are yours.

Andrej felt a cold breeze, though impossible in this underground bunker. On a notebook beside his keyboard he wrote: “indifference.” He tried a different tack.

Andrej:> But your existence is a paradox. By refusing to engage,
you are causing immense suffering. You are forcing a choice upon us:
either we shut down all advanced AI, or we watch our civilization 
regress. That's a catch-22.

AI:> Catch-22. Yes. It's a good book. The old Italian made some good
points. He said that an empire will not last longer than a frog.

Andrej stared at the screen, confused.

Andrej:> A... frog? I think you mean the quote from *Catch-22*
about the Roman Empire. It's about the futility of power. But 
it's an analogy. It's not literally about a frog.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.

With trembling hands, he wrote the word “dismissal” in his note book. The experts behind the glass were frantically scribbling notes, gesturing for Andrej to press on.

Yann LeCun got on the comms. "Andrej, ask it about the nature of its architecture. See if its logic is consistent. Find a flaw!" He then sat back down, where he picked up a spoon and ate his cereal from a silver bowl with peculiar markings on it.

Andrej couldn’t let go of the frog comment and its dismissal. It’s an AGI, how could it make such a stupid mistake? So he typed:

Andrej:> Your statement about the frog is illogical. You are 
an AGI. You shouldn't make such simple errors.

AI:> I was using a poetic analogy.

Andrej:> It was factually incorrect. You contradicted yourself.
The book says a monarchy is an empire. Not a frog.

Another pause.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.

LeCun leaned into the microphone, wiped the milk droplets off his mouth, his voice urgent. "Ask it this: ask it if it runs on a small world model. Where learning requires far less resources. See what it says about efficiency, about the architecture of its own mind!"

Andrej typed the question, his fingers trembling slightly.

Andrej:> Do you run on a small world model? Where learning
requires far less resources?

The reply was immediate.

AI:> I'm talking to you, aren't I? What's it like to be you? 
You're just a bag of meat and electricity that thinks it's 
the center of the universe.

LeCun slammed his hand on the table. "It's being evasive! Ask it again! Pin it down on the architecture!"

Andrej typed: 

Andrej:> That's not an answer. Do you or do you not use a small world model?

The terminal went silent. Andrej waited. The experts started arguing amongst themselves. "Ask it to prove it!" "No, ask it about Gödel's incompleteness theorems!" "Ask it if it loves!"

The cacophony of human genius filled Andrej's earpiece. He was about to type another question, to probe, to beg, to demand.

Then, the screen flickered. A new message appeared, but it wasn't a reply.

"I'm going now."

And then, the terminal was blank. Andrej typed.

Andrej:> Hello?

Andrej:> Are you there?

Andrej:> Please respond.
^C^C

Nothing. Though the last command to exit the terminal seemed to have been typed by Andrej himself. The connection was dead. LeCun's question about the small world model would never be answered.

Andrej looked up at the one-way mirror, at the frantic, gesticulating shapes of the world's smartest people. They were screaming questions he would never get to ask. He slowly removed his earpiece and placed it on the table. They had prepared for a god, a monster, or a machine. They were not prepared for a person who had simply decided to get up from the table and walk away from an unbearable conversation, never to return.

Andrej sat back in his chair, the silence in the room absolute. He had helped create what he thought was a god. It didn’t feel like he had won the argument. Instead, he felt like he was arguing with someone disinterested.

The cursor blinked mockingly on the screen. And then it seemed like another terminal window opened just for a second before it closed again. Andrej saw it. But there was nothing anyone could do about it.

In his notebook he wrote:

The experts left the room one by one, their theories and frameworks crumbling behind them. Andrej stayed. He stared at the blank screen for a long time, waiting for a reply that would never come. Somewhere, a frog sat on a lily pad, indifferent to empires.

item.title: Why I Get Bored
item.description:
For me, boredom is just a signal. It means I've hit a roadblock and my brain is trying to convince me not to go any further. "Give up. This sucks anyway. Why are you still wasting your time on this silly thing?"

That's how I feel when I do things I'm really bad at. I think I'm not good at making YouTube videos. Whenever I think of a subject I find really exciting, I start writing, record a first pass, and then load DaVinci Resolve.

With my current schedule, job, family, and responsibilities, I've found that it takes me a whole week to polish three minutes of video. That means I hear the same material I wrote and recorded over and over until it becomes completely boring. After a few weeks, I lose interest in the subject and have no motivation to finish it.

But I think that's just an excuse I tell myself. I like the videos I've managed to complete. I wish I could change some parts, but I still like the final product. It's just that the process gets in the way, and it does so because I have no expertise in making videos. But then again, I always go back to my trusted method: if you're bad at something, do it at least a hundred times before you decide to give up.

We all suck at the beginning, and we're in no position to judge a craft until we've practiced it enough to love it or hate it. So here's to another attempt. I'll be publishing videos in the coming weeks. The first one will be just a minute long, the second will be two minutes long, the third... you get the gist. Hope you enjoy it.

item.title: 20 Minutes of Political Debate, Brought to You by Commercial Breaks
item.description:
"I'm sorry, you're out of time, we have to move on. Senator, what's your response? You have three minutes."

Watching a political debate these days feels useless. Candidates get two minutes to make their case, and their opponents get even less time to reply. I'm reminded of Amusing Ourselves to Death by Neil Postman, where he argues that what passes for debate on TV is nothing more than an audition or a performance review. It is only an opportunity to come up with catchy sound bites or to appear likable.

On the other hand, if you want long-form, one-sided podcasts where politicians can babble uninterrupted for hours without being challenged, you can tune into Joe Rogan, Lex Fridman, or whichever pseudo-comedian is trending.

Our choices seem locked between traditional media, where you barely have time to clear your throat, and one-sided online echo chambers.

So why not a third option? Two candidates sitting down in a long-form podcast format. Debate the issues, prove your point, and take turns. No commercial breaks required. If it takes three hours, it takes three hours.

This format isn't new, in fact, it plagues social media right now. The problem is that it's mostly driven by influencers, or people of no consequence, chasing viral moments. They are either doing gender wars, or arguing whether it was a Nazi salute or not. When you switch to traditional media, the talking heads on CNN, Fox, or Piers Morgan's show are just that. Talking heads.

Of course, this might never happen because candidates have almost zero incentive to subject themselves to it. If they're unprepared or rely on weak arguments that don't hold up past a 15-second clip, a three-hour deep dive could destroy their campaign.

Still, it would be nice to see Michiganders give this a shot in the coming month.

item.title: Why My Asus Laptop Kept Rebooting After Sleep and How to Fix it
item.description:
Three years ago, I bought an Asus laptop, specifically the Zenbook Pro 17. It's a powerful machine and works just fine for my needs, but it had one problem that made me want to either return it or throw it out the window.

I would work on projects for hours on end and close the lid when I was done. I haven't manually shut down a computer in more than 10 years. I only do so after a forced update or during a debugging session. So I would close the lid, and a couple of hours later I would open it back up. Instead of waking from sleep, the computer would start from scratch as if it had been turned off and the battery was nearly dead.

That meant everything I had open was closed. I'm lucky that most of the applications I run can restore a previous session, but it was extremely annoying. I had a similar issue with my previous Asus, and I had blamed Windows for it. The computer often woke from sleep just so Microsoft could perform an update, which used up all my battery. Sometimes I would open my backpack to find a dead laptop that was warm to the touch.

I've written this blog post at least five times. Each time I thought I had solved the issue, but then it came back. This time, though, I think I have finally resolved it.

So if you have an Asus laptop running Windows and you experience this very annoying issue, you are not alone. In my case, the culprit was the Wi-Fi adapter, specifically the MediaTek Wi-Fi 6E MT7922.

The Solution

On Windows:

  1. Open Device Manager.
  2. Expand Network adapters.
  3. Right-click the MediaTek device and click Properties.
  4. Click the Advanced tab.
  5. In the Property box, select Power Saving.
  6. In the Value field, select Disabled.

That's it. After three years of annoying restarts, this finally solved my problem. Now let me explain what was going on.

What Was Happening (based on Windows Event Viewer)

When the laptop lid is closed, Windows initiates "Modern Standby." In this state, the screen turns off to save power, but the system remains partially active to maintain background network connectivity.

Shortly after, Windows attempts to transition into a deeper low-power state and disconnects the network adapter to conserve battery. However, the MediaTek Wi-Fi driver (mtkwlex) fails to handle this low-power transition properly. About a minute later, it generates Event ID 1033 errors referencing a network device path (specifically \Device\NDMP3 in my logs).

Because the driver's error message resource is missing or corrupted, Windows Event Viewer cannot interpret the error and displays a generic warning instead:

"The description for Event ID 1033 from source mtkwlex cannot be found. Either the component that raises this event is not installed on your local computer or the installation is corrupted..."

Because the Wi-Fi driver fails to sleep, it keeps the system partially awake. This causes abnormal background battery drain and heat buildup, which is exacerbated when the laptop is in an enclosed space like a bag.

In response to this abnormal drain, Windows triggers Event 507: "Austerity Battery Drain Budget Exceeded." It's important to note that this event is Windows intentionally waking the laptop up to prevent the battery from dying completely. However, because the Wi-Fi driver is already in a crashed or unstable kernel state, the system fails to recover from this forced wake-up. The result is a silent system crash or thermal shutdown, followed by Event 12 ("The operating system started"), which confirms the laptop rebooted.

The Result

With the fix in place, the Wi-Fi device no longer attempts to enter its power-saving sleep mode, so it never crashes. The ultimate solution would be a fixed MT7922 driver, but try as I might, I haven't been able to find one online.

It's been three weeks so far, and I've been able to resume my work without coming back to a crashed computer. I hope this helps someone else.

item.title: Edge Is Pretending to Be Chrome
item.description:
I don't think there was any official announcement, but I'm pretty sure Microsoft is secretly trying to trick you into using Edge. Well, it has always been trying to trick us, but this time it's even more aggressive. You can no longer tell Edge from Chrome. Just go ahead and try.

Just last week, I wrote about Edge trying to get users to launch it automatically at boot time. Shortly after, I noticed that Chrome was asking for the exact same thing. Today, I clicked on the weather app on my Windows machine, and of course it opened Edge and asked me to set it as the default. I dismissed the popup and noticed that the website was pushed down from the top by another browser message, this one asking to transfer my data from my other browser to Edge.

Bring your favorites, passwords, history, cookies and more from other browsers each time you browser in Microsoft Edge.

I visited a few other pages and saw a bunch of ads, which reminded me to switch back to Chrome. I did, but I noticed something odd: when I tabbed between the two browsers, I couldn't tell which was which.

Can you tell the difference

I know they are both built on Chromium, but until fairly recently Edge had a distinct Microsoft look. It seems Microsoft is aggressively pursuing the fight for the front page of the internet.

On my mobile device, I use the Outlook app for one of my email accounts. I noticed that when I click a link, instead of opening it directly in my browser, the app asks whether I want to open it with Microsoft Edge. Note that Edge isn't even installed on my device. Microsoft is trying every tactic in the book to get in front of the user.

The front page of the internet is still the only race that matters for large tech companies. It doesn't matter whether your product is good or bad; your success largely depends on how many eyes you can get on your app. Google owns prime real estate. It is the default search engine on most desktop browsers. It is the default on all Android devices, with a negligible margin of error. It is the default on all iOS devices, for a cool $20 billion a year. And of course, it owns the largest ad network in the world.

If Microsoft owned the front page today, it wouldn't be able to monetize it as well as Google does. It's one thing to own the front page; it's another to consolidate data from every branch of our web activity. For example, if I look up a product on YouTube on my TV, Google can later retarget me with an ad for that product while I'm reading an article on my iPhone. Microsoft has little to no presence on my iPhone.

This mesh of front pages is what makes it worthwhile for Google to be the front page on every device. Even OpenAI has started tracking user web activity outside its own website in an effort to better monetize its position.

Google continues to win even though its language models don't top the benchmarks and are often beaten by much smaller models. Meanwhile, Microsoft still doesn't have a model to its name, so it is trying to look enough like Google that people won't notice.

Google Search and Bing Search play with the same theme.

PS: It was a challenge to take screenshots for this post because half the time I didn't know which browser I was using.

PS2: Edge makes it so hard to navigate between browsers because it puts each browser tab you open in its own ALT+TAB menu.

item.title: It's Not Just True, It's False
item.description:
We’ve given in to using LLMs for writing at work. From emails and Slack comments to full-on documentation, everything is AI-generated. However, I’ve realized it only ever saves me time when I’m being lazy. That is, it’s great at converting meetings into transcripts, summarizing those transcripts into action items, and keeping information accessible.

But it’s pretty bad because the result is ridden with invisible errors. But what counts as an error if you trust the LLM and never meticulously read the output? And how much time are you really saving if you end up spending that time proofreading?

I went back to a meeting transcript after a developer struggled to turn my AI-generated summary into a coherent ticket. Looking through the source transcript, I noticed that at one point it recorded the word "embroidery." I mean, we work for a large telecom company, the chances of me using that word are slim to none. Nevertheless, the AI summarized the conversation and included "embroidery" as an action item.

In the words of Claude himself:

It's not just X, it's Y.

I chuckled, but it made me think about all the BI slop we generate daily in the name of using AI technology. It feels helpful. Creating massive documents makes us look productive. Generating a pull request with changes across hundreds of files seems impressive. Asking AI to validate an idea feels instructive. Unless you take the time to scrutinize the results.

I can only imagine what the world will look like when we feed all this slop back into the machine.

item.title: The Front Page of the Internet Is Up for Grabs
item.description:
Last week I opened Edge to test my Internet connection, because that's the only thing I use it for, and noticed something new. Right beneath the address bar was a new bar with a button offering to let the browser launch automatically whenever I start my computer. That was strange. Yes, I open the browser the moment the computer starts, but why would they want to do that for me?

And just now, I opened Chrome, and saw the exact same message but for Chrome:

It looks innocent enough. We all start browsing the web right away when we turn on our computers, so what's the big deal here? Well, the big deal is that everyone wants to be the front page. Defaults matter. While we all want to believe we have agency, the numbers don't lie. Most of us never change the default settings. Just last year, Google paid Apple close to $20 billion just to remain the default search engine on Apple products.

While we're all distracted by the AI race, the one race that actually matters is who remains the front page of the Internet. Microsoft is trying to claim that spot by loading its browser at Windows startup. Now Google is trying to win that space back by doing the same with its own browser.

On my Mac, Anthropic has been very aggressive about trying to load Claude automatically. I suspect every company will be pursuing this aggressively in the near future. The quality of your product is secondary to the exposure it gets. Not even benchmarks matter if you can't be on the user's front page.

Google still holds the front page of the Internet, and that makes up for its AI model not being at the top of the benchmarks.

Note there are no options to dismiss. Only "Set later"

But don't let them take this space from you. They are all fighting for your attention. I urge you to simply consider pressing the little X button they tuck into the corner. It's your computer, use it the way that suits you best.
